ME/CFS has no cure and, in routine care, no biomarker. That combination makes the consultation itself the highest-risk moment in the disease: the patient arrives carrying years of research and years of dismissal, the doctor arrives with twelve minutes and no textbook answer, and both sides pattern-match the other into a caricature — "Dr. Google" versus "the doctor who doesn't believe me." This series is about what actually happens in that room, and how to keep the relationship alive anyway.

Why this matters more than in most diseases: for an incurable condition, **continuity of care is itself a treatment.** Losing a doctor is not an inconvenience — it means losing disability documentation, referrals, red-flag screening, and medication stewardship, all at once.

---

## The two articles

Read the one written for your side of the desk — or both, if you want to understand the other side.

### For patients: when you know more than your doctor

**[When Your Doctor Doesn't Know Your Disease](../patient-doctor-relationship/when-your-doctor-doesnt-know-your-disease/index.qmd)** — why the conflict is structural rather than personal; the knowledge asymmetry stated honestly in both directions; the trust death spiral that can end with no doctor at all; and ten concrete tactics for using your research as a tool instead of a weapon — send before you spring, separate observation from interpretation, ask for the decision rather than the agreement, and never leave a doctor without knowing where the next one is.

### For doctors and caregivers: the informed patient

**[Why Your Patient Knows So Much](../patient-doctor-relationship/why-your-patient-knows-so-much/index.qmd)** — why self-research is a rational adaptation to a system that said "we have nothing for you"; what the consultation research says about internet-informed patients; scripts for the three patients you will meet (the well-sourced, the fragile-logic, the desperate); why saying "I don't know" protects your authority; and the caregiver's working role as amplifier, not advocate-at-war.

---

## A note on honesty

This series argues from the structure of the situation and cites the consultation, stigma, and patient-experience literature where it exists. It deliberately avoids fabricating numbers: where a claim about doctor–patient conflict is not quantified in studies, it is stated as structural reasoning, not statistics. The underlying medical science is fully cited in the primary document [@Loth2026mecfs].
